doc.title: Rick Montalbano interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 12, 2011

title: Valuing melody phrasing like Sinatra
summary: He likes players who render a melody with conversational phrasing, and he comments on over-hyped modern music and his own stillness at the piano.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What about musical, even specifically musical things that you like in other players. Is it possible to put it into words?

Well probably part of it. I would say one of the things I really like is people who can play a melody, render a melody, phrase it with beautiful conversational type phrasing, you know, like a Sinatra phrasing let’s say. I’d say if every musician would sit down with those Sinatra records and literally copy his phrasing, the breathing points and the bigger curve of his phrasing, I think everyone would sound better. You know there’s a lot of concentration on just soloing and the eighth notes and immediately into that aspect and not as much on, you know, playing a melody the right way, and not the way it appears in a book. You know the way certain words take more time and so you borrow from something and rubato I guess, but even when you’re playing in time, if you play literally what are in those books when you’re playing standards, it would sound ridiculous. So © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-
yeah, I look for that, somebody with a sound and a feel and a touch, who can really play a beautiful melody. And of course solo, but, you know.
I remember you making a comment once about, I think it was Al Jarreau, and you were irked by — don’t get up —
That it was too affected. Everything had to have like something extra, or something like that. He couldn’t just leave it alone.

Yeah. I guess. I don’t remember specifically saying it. I probably did. I probably said a lot of ridiculous things. But yeah, I think in general music today is so hyped up and, you know, everything has got to be bigger than life. People need something. It was funny my sister, my dearest sister, my older sister, the other day we were in a group of people and we were talking about music and somebody playing or somebody on TV and the way they expressed themselves, and she said “Rick, you used to move so much when you played, you really felt the music. And now you don’t move at all.” Uh yeah, thanks. You know, and I guess when I see some people film, I feel like I’m just planted there and it’s all, I don’t move. I move my fingers and I sit there. RB: I’ve got a question.
